line: Catalog is immaculate Still runnin’ the game, don’t ask me about the practice
vault_lines: Still runnin' the game, don't ask me about the practice
meaning:
Describing his dominance over the rap industry, Drake references NBA Hall of Famer Allen Iverson’s infamous “practice” press conference from 2002. When a reporter asked Iverson about missing one practice, he expressed his displeasure at the question, responding with the following:

We’re talking about practice. Not a game! Not a game! Not a game! We’re talking about practice. Not a game; not the game that I go out there and die for and play every game like it’s my last, not the game, we’re talking about practice, man. I mean, how silly is that? We’re talking about practice.

As a basketball icon and NBA MVP, Iverson was upset that his premier status and willingness to practice were called into question. The lengthy nature of Iverson’s response also may have been triggered by the murder of his best friend, Rahsaan Langeford, seven months prior to the press conference. Like AI, Drake finds that his position or “run” atop the rap game will only continue and that “running” in practice is not of other’s concern.

line: Patti LaBelle, who knew that we would sell pies?
vault_lines: Patti LaBelle, who knew that we would sell pies?
meaning:
Patti LaBelle is an American R&B and Soul artist known for  songs such as “If Only You Knew” and “On My Own.” In 2015, she began selling sweet potato pies at Walmart stores throughout the United States. Following a viral review from social media personality James Wright, the pies quickly sold out. In the years following the video, the pies continue to be a commercial success, with more than 36,000 sold each day.

Ross uses pies as a double entendre to reference Patti LaBelle’s sweet potato dessert and drug trafficking. A pie is a slang term for a kilogram of cocaine, an amount which he expresses disbelief in his ability to sell. Ross himself drew his rap name from drug kingpin “Freeway” Ricky Ross, who established an extensive distribution network throughout Los Angeles in the 1980s and ‘90s.

line: Ho, you go on vacation, don’t ask me about relaxin’ Not sure if you know but I’m actually Michael Jackson The man I see in the mirror is actually goin’ platinum
vault_lines: Ho, you go on vacation, don't ask me about relaxin'
meaning:
Drake compares his success in the music industry to legendary pop icon Michael Jackson. Jackson is remembered today for his live performances, his memorable record releases and the consistency of his music after departing from the The Jackson 5 group to start a solo career. After the King of Pop’s untimely death in 2009, his legacy was succeeded by his posthumous music, including his appearance on Drake’s 2018 album Scorpion, on the track “Don’t Matter to Me.” The song samples a once unreleased Jackson track and highlighted the similarity of both singers' careers. In 2016, Drake broke MJ’s record for most American Music Award nominations, establishing both as significant figures at the top of their respective genres.

Interestingly enough, Drake boasts an appearance on the 2016 2 Chainz track “Big Amount,” rapping:

Michael Jackson talkin' to me in my dreams
And he say, “You bad and you know it”
Better shamone with my check then
I’m a J. Prince investment

In those lines, Drake mentions the hit 1987 single “Bad,” similar to how he slyly mentions Jackson’s “Man in the Mirror” from 1988 on this track. Here, Drake uses the track’s title to boast his countless platinum certifications and is crowned as the top certified singles artist of the RIAA.

Charles “Charlie” Brown is the principal character of the comic strip Peanuts, syndicated in daily and Sunday newspapers in numerous countries worldwide. Depicted as a “lovable loser,” Charlie Brown is one of the great American archetypes and a popular and widely recognized cartoon character. Charlie Brown is characterized as a person who frequently suffers, and as a result, is usually nervous and lacks self-confidence. He shows both pessimistic and optimistic attitudes: on some days, he is apprehensive to even go outside because his day might just be spoiled, but on others, he hopes for the best and tries as much as he can to accomplish things. He is easily recognized by his trademark zigzag patterned shirt.

The character’s creator, Charles M. Schulz, said that Charlie Brown “has to be the one who suffers, because he is a caricature of the average person. Most of us are much more acquainted with losing than we are with winning.” Despite this, Charlie Brown does not always suffer, as he has experienced some happy moments and victories through the years, and he has sometimes uncharacteristically shown self-assertiveness despite his frequent nervousness. Schulz also said: “I like to have Charlie Brown eventually be the focal point of almost every story.” Charlie Brown is the only Peanuts character to have appeared regularly in the strip throughout its entire 50-year run.

line: No socks, no shoes, I put my soul in it
vault_lines: No socks, no shoes, I put my soul in it
meaning:
The line “No socks, no shoes, I put my soul in it” is deceptively simple but richly metaphorical, blending physical imagery with emotional depth. On the surface, it paints an image of bare feet—raw, exposed, grounded—a choice that immediately suggests vulnerability and authenticity. By stating “no socks, no shoes,” Tyler implies he’s stripped of protection, artifice, or barriers, offering something unfiltered and direct. This lack of footwear can symbolize humility or returning to basics, almost like standing barefoot on the earth—fully present and connected to something real.

The brilliance comes in the wordplay between “soul” and “sole.” Shoes typically have soles, but Tyler says he has no shoes—just his soul. It’s a pun that links physical absence to spiritual presence: even without the material (the soles), he’s putting everything internal (his soul) into what he’s doing. That twist suggests total emotional investment, the idea that what he’s delivering—whether a verse, a relationship, or a performance—isn’t polished or dressed up, but deeply personal and fully committed. It’s a mic-drop moment of poetic minimalism that blends swagger, sacrifice, and sincerity in a single bar.

This came as a huge shock to people, considering the Suns had the best record in the NBA’s regular season and had made it to the finals the previous year.

Wayne himself attended the game in support of the Suns and their point guard Chris Paul, a close friend of his. Additionally, the rapper had already taunted the Mavericks earlier on in the season, calling their star player Luka Dončić a “ho” through a tweet.

meaning:
Kanye is poking fun at Stump’s notoriously difficult-to-understand delivery, low key referencing the misheard lyrics videos that went viral in March ’07 as the original FOB song got Top 40 airplay; Kanye was one of the thousands of people who had no idea what the hell Stump was saying, no matter how many times they heard the song (“Also into cats, also into cats").

Though, Kanye isn’t just baffled by the song’s delivery. The content, too, seems absurd. The title and refrain “this ain’t a scene, it’s a goddamn arms race” invokes a longing for a scene that isn’t so competitive, that isn’t “so addicted and obsessed with new arts, cultures and loves”, but Kanye, fighting for recognition not just as a producer but also as a rapper and celebrating the intense competition that has been vital to hip-hop since day one, has never known a scene that isn’t an arms race.

To ask for a scene that’s less competitive, less obsessed with creating new forms of art and breaking down barriers between arts and cultures, is to bite the hand that feeds. Certainly, FOB wouldn’t have “raced straight to the top” if they didn’t satisfy this very desire for newness, if they didn’t make a new weapon, and isn’t that exactly what this remix is? Kanye knows it.

line: Life from the 504 It’s Mr. Crazy flow Jumping like a bungee, no rope Even in the dungeon I glow Even if it ain’t sunny I glow If it ain’t about money I go Nowhere, I’m nailed to the flo’ I am a sail to the water, money’s the sail to my boat And it’s going down, it’s going down Like there’s a whale in the boat And you can smell what I smoke And yep, I sip that lean You hit me with that combination that make my eyes bleed I’m a shark in the water Yeah, I swim with the big So I don’t have time to deal with Willy the Squid L-L-Lilly pad homies L-L-Look at the monster Man, you don’t want to crash Like La-La-La Bamba See it’s me, Roney, and Terry And my new drop is berry Watermelon, plum Just call it fruit punch I’m an old rapper Getting new bucks And all you new rappers You’re just new lunch Flow sick So sick Need a Doc, yes A creature Monster Like the Loch Ness I gets hotter by the tick Before I sizzle to death I just tell the clock “Gimme a sec” I’m the middle of the war, where my enemy at? I’m runnin’ it like Eric Eric Bieniemy back I hit a track I’m like an energy pack The instruments are crying out “Where the sympathy at?” Okay, I’m finna be that Whatever rich look like, well look I’m finna be that They say money ain’t everything But I look better than that It’s Cash Money Young money Have a sweater with that And just chill
vault_lines: Nowhere, I'm nailed to the flo'
meaning:
This verse is Lil Wayne showing off his wordplay, wealth, status, and nonstop “crazy” flow. Almost every few lines connect through puns or an extended metaphor.

“Life from the 504 / It’s Mr. Crazy Flow”

The 504 is the New Orleans area code, identifying Wayne with his hometown. “Mr. Crazy Flow” introduces the verse as a lyrical exhibition.

“Jumping like a bungee, no rope”

His flow and energy are “jumping,” but without a rope, the image becomes reckless and dangerous, matching his wild persona.

“Even in the dungeon I glow / Even if it ain’t sunny I glow”

Even in darkness, hardship, or confinement, he still shines through his talent, jewelry, and celebrity.

“If it ain’t about money I go / Nowhere, I’m nailed to the flo’”

He initially makes it sound like he will leave if money isn’t involved, then flips it: he goes nowhere because he refuses to move unless money is involved.

“I am a sail to the water, money’s the sail to my boat”

The wording is intentionally slippery. Money is what catches the wind and propels his life forward, the way a sail moves a boat.

“And it’s going down… / Like there’s a whale in the boat”

“It’s going down” means something major is happening, but Wayne turns it literal: a whale’s weight would make the boat sink.

“And you can smell what I smoke / And yep, I sip that lean”

References to marijuana and lean, a recreational mixture usually involving prescription cough syrup and soda.

“You hit me with that combination that make my eyes bleed”

The combination of smoking and lean makes his eyes extremely red. “Combination” can also sound like a series of punches causing physical injury.

“I’m a shark in the water / Yeah, I swim with the big”

Wayne presents himself as a powerful predator who operates alongside the biggest names in the industry.

“So I don’t have time to deal with Willy the Squid”

A playful contrast with the shark imagery. “Willy” likely combines associations with Free Willy and a weak, insignificant sea creature. He doesn’t waste time on small-time rappers.

“L-L-Lilly pad homies, L-L-Look at the monster”

The stuttering repetition makes the delivery sound frantic. His rivals are tiny frogs sitting on lily pads while he is a sea monster.

“Man, you don’t want to crash / Like La-La-La Bamba”

A dark reference to “La Bamba” singer Ritchie Valens, who died in a plane crash. The repeated syllables also continue the stuttering rhyme pattern.

“See, it’s me, Roney, and Terry / And my new drop is berry / Watermelon, plum / Just call it fruit punch”

He names his companions and describes a brightly colored drop-top car. The berry, watermelon, and plum colors combine into “fruit punch.” “Punch” may also preserve the verse’s aggressive tone.

“I’m an old rapper / Getting new bucks”

Although he had already been rapping for years, he continued making fresh money and staying relevant.

“And all you new rappers / You’re just new lunch”

The newer rappers are not competition, they are fresh prey for Wayne to devour.

“Flow sick / So sick / Need a Doc, yes”

His flow is “sick,” meaning excellent, but the next line treats the sickness literally: he needs a doctor.

“A creature / Monster / Like the Loch Ness”

He compares himself to the legendary Loch Ness Monster—rare, frightening, and almost beyond belief.

“I gets hotter by the tick / Before I sizzle to death / I just tell the clock / ‘Gimme a sec’”

His performance becomes hotter with every tick of the clock. “Give me a sec” means give him a second, but he is literally addressing the clock and requesting more time before he overheats.

“I’m the middle of the war, where my enemy at?”

Rap is presented as warfare, and Wayne is actively searching for challengers instead of avoiding them.

“I’m runnin’ it like Eric, Eric Bieniemy back”

Eric Bieniemy was a football running back. Wayne is “running” the rap game like Bieniemy ran the football; the repeated first name also strengthens the rhythm.

“I hit a track, I’m like an energy pack”

When Wayne enters a song, he injects it with immediate energy, like a battery or power pack.

“The instruments are crying out, ‘Where the sympathy at?’”

He attacks the beat so aggressively that the instruments are personified as crying and begging for mercy.

“Okay, I’m finna be that / Whatever rich look like, well look, I’m finna be that”

“Finna” means “fixing to” or “about to.” Whatever image represents wealth, Wayne intends to become its living definition.

“They say money ain’t everything / But I look better than that”

He twists the familiar saying. Money may not be everything, but being wealthy looks much better than being without it.

“It’s Cash Money / Young Money / Have a sweater with that / And just chill”

Cash Money is his original record label, and Young Money is his own imprint. A sweater keeps someone warm, while “chill” means relax, ending the verse with a temperature joke after repeatedly describing himself as hot.

line: Told her gettin’ out the game is like coming out of a coma I’m trying,
vault_lines: Told her gettin' out the game is like coming out of a coma
meaning:
In three ways, Wayne use a coma to describe his experience of living the street life (i.e., “the game”) and attempting to get out of it.

(1) Wayne tells his mother that “coming out of the game is like coming out of a coma,” forming an analogy to underscore the low chances he has of escaping the street life. For reference, approximately 30-50% of medically diagnosed comatose persons “wake up."

(2) Wayne explains he is “trying”; however, the simile of escaping the game and rising from a coma illustrates that his attempts are futile—Wayne “trying” to escape the game is like a person “trying” to wake up from a coma. A person unfortunately cannot “try,” in a traditional sense, to wake up from a coma.

(3) This also demonstrates the principle of “mind over matter.” Despite lacking most of their faculties, people in comas oftentimes have limited forms of consciousness. By “trying” to wake up from a coma, the comatose person inherently has a positive/hopeful mindset, and that mindset might give them a greater chance of recovering. Similarly, even though Wayne’s literal “trying” won’t get him out of the game, his positive/hopeful mindset might.

Wayne is a fan of the “lane” metaphor, and has used it to mean a car lane (“Jazz Cartier”), a basketball lane (“Outstanding”), and even as a bowling lane (“Hawaii 5.0”).

The results of trying to take over someone else’s lane usually lead to a collision. Combined with the injunction to not fuck with him implies that in any collision, you will be the one who gets totaled. Just don’t. Fuck. With. Lil. Wayne.

Wayne often references “the crossroads,” mentioning it explicitly during “After Disaster,” and “Ready For The World”:

If you are choking on a chunk of charcoal instead of using it to start a fire to keep warm, then you must really like pain.

line: I get stoked, might choke Like I chewed a chunk of charcoal,
vault_lines: I get stoked, might choke
meaning:
“If I get stung I get stoked” is basically Wayne saying if he gets ‘stung’ (very drunk off large amounts of alcohol), he gets ‘stoked’, by which he likely means high on marijuana. He then implies that he might be going into anaphylaxis because of the jellyfish sting.

This is also more tightly packed alliteration:
 “might choke like I chewed a chunk of charcoal.”

Charcoal is black residue mixed with ashes that is often created by burning wood. It’s definitely not something you would want in your mouth in large amounts, the taste and texture alone would be unpalatable. However, people do “chew charcoal” to help with overdoses of various kinds, though the efficacy of doing so is in question.

Charcoal is important when building (stoking) a fire, as it’s these pieces that will hold heat and cook food or provide long periods of warmth.

While ‘fool’ and ‘dummy’ are direct synonyms, ‘dummy’ is another word for ‘pacifier’, a baby’s toy that it can suck on in times of distress. So he’s saying he is a “sucker for pain.”

Slitting his throat will already kill him, so cutting his head off is unnecessary pain that he’s a “fool” for.

Drake explained this lyric in a 2009 interview with MTV News:


When I was going through the creative process for So Far Gone, I was actually at a pretty dark place in my life. It was a frustrating time for my family, because my grandmother—who is now in her mid- to late 90s—was just losing it. It was hard for my mother to watch. And it was just, it was really at a point where it was like, ‘Is this rap thing going to work?’ Like, ‘Is this my choice? Is this what I am committing to?’ Money was an issue. Degrassi had ended years ago, and we were just all kind of trying to figure stuff out.

So my mother was going through a rough time. And yeah, man, one night she just broke down and tried to actually run away from the house, tried to leave it all behind. It was just a lot going on, and she never would have really left. She would’ve always come back, but it was just a frustrating moment for her. So I had forgot something in my car, and I came outside and I saw bags sitting by her car. I saw her out there, and she just started crying right away when she saw me. Anyway, I don’t wanna get too emotional, but I had to hug her. My father doesn’t stay with us, so I had to be security for her and just let her know that everything is going to be all right.

Guerrilla Warfare is the second studio album by the New Orleans hip-hop group Hot Boys, released July 27, 1999 on Cash Money Records. The Hot Boys highly anticipated sophomore effort, Guerrilla Warfare, issued after Cash Money’s distribution deal with Universal Records, was an instant hit. It debuted at #5 on the Billboard 200 and #1 on the Top R&B/Hip Hop Albums selling 142,000 copies in its first week,[6] and remains their most successful album as a group and with Cash Money Records.

The common grading scale is a system of recognition for performance in a class, with the best results being an A+ grade and the worst result being a Fail (F). At most schools, an F is earned after a student gets scores from 0% to 59% in a class, equivalent to a 0 GPA.



Wayne relates this to his attitude, as “don’t give a F” is an abbreviated slang of “Don’t give a fuck,” meaning Wayne does not care about his poor grades or the consequences that come with failing.

Wayne dropped out of school at age 14 to focus on creating music, although he was an honors student before abandoning his education.

line: You out of work, I know it’s tough
vault_lines: You out of work, I know it's tough
meaning: In 2008 due to a lawsuit with Brookland Ent. more popularly known as, (Trackmasters) a judge ruled that Lil' Kim could not make new music. It remains unclear how long Lil' Kim was contractually barred from making new music, but it’s widely speculated that it lasted from 2008-2016. During this time Lil' Kim did a track with Birdman which also featured Nicki Minaj and she accused them of using the track to stamp Nicki Minaj’s career and discard her as old news. After the track’s official release Lil' Kim would fall out with her contacts at Cash Money. While she alleges shady business on their end, it’s speculated that her failure to disclose her legal woes (being barred from making new music) are the true cause of the fallout. Here with “You out of work, I know it’s tough” Nicki Minaj leans into the idea that her and the rest of the Cash Money team became privy to Lil' Kim’s legal troubles. At this time Lil' Kim , a contestant on “Dancing With The Stars” would still drop mixtapes and tracks dissing Minaj but did not have any commercial music release until 2019.

Like the rest of the Young Money crew and many other rappers these days, Nicki Minaj is known for using what’s called hashtag rap. This song is probably her most obvious and famous display of the technique.

My role in hip-hop has been super unique because when my first album came out, there had been so much time where there wasn’t a female rap album out that went platinum. There wasn’t a big female rap presence right before I got in. So, my role was reintroducing the female rapper to pop culture. 

Shortly after the interview, Nicki clarified her thoughts after hearing confusion from fans in an Instagram post:

When I came out, there had been a drought of a few years where NO female rap album had gone platinum, females weren’t getting budgets, the industry did NOT believe in the female rapper anymore. They had stopped generating MONEY for labels. Ask any rap historian or just anyone with a brain. These are facts and nothing but the facts. So I “REINTRODUCED” the “successful” female rapper back to POP CULTURE. Showed big business we were major players in the game just like the boys were.

Once her career took off, Nicki became the first female rapper to top the Billboard 200 in nine years, the first female to chart at #1 on the Hot Rap Songs for seven years, and her first album broke the first-week sales for a female rap album, certainly bringing female rappers on the “map again.”

Nicki spoke about a similar issue on her 2010 track “Roman’s Revenge:”

line: To the ladies havin’ babies without no drama To my niggas with figgas say “I love my baby mama”
vault_lines: To the ladies havin' babies without no drama
meaning:
In this song Mannie Fresh and the other Cash Money Millionaires summarize the male fantasy of wealth, power, and women who throw themselves at them, while minimizing concerns that their actions or their focus has any negative impact on the women and children that they primarily objectify. The most interesting couplet in the rap due to various interpretations is  “ladies havin’ babies without no drama / To my niggas with figgas say ‘I love my baby mama.’” This and other themes are explored.

Mannie Fresh’s first verse, when understood as an oral persuasive essay, uses the technique of first addressing detractors. A listener that may not appreciate the overall tone may conclude, incorrectly in Mannie’s view, that the rappers are exploiting these women. But Mannie Fresh in this rhetorical device makes a case for greater respect for women than the rest of the song suggests. While the women in the song are considered primarily on their sexual promiscuity, Mannie here seeks to let us know that he knows them by name and wants to shout out who they are: “Deshawn, Eshlawn, Lil Mama….” He repeats that he loves them for emphasis: “I love y'all broads.” He loves them so much that he reassures his “dawgs” that he means “no disrespect.” Then he evaluates if there were a coerced relationship then there would be “drama,” but the women here are having babies “without no drama.” For those financially well-off, the Cash Money Millionaires, or similar men, note that they “love my baby mama.” Mannie further explains that he provides for them financially in ways that exceeds what a typical baby’s daddy would provide: paying for tattoos and breast implants. It’s worth noting that Juvenile, a member of the Cash Money Millionaires who raps later in the song, was arrested in 2017 for failing to pay $170,000 in child support.

In an entire song describing sexual acts and what women will give to him sexually Mannie Fresh notes that the relationship if it were untoward would result in “drama.” At an initial glance, “ladies havin' babies without no drama” seems to express some degree of women’s liberation and that the women have a choice in this matter. Perhaps Mannie supposes that a well-supported, independent woman may choose to have a child and with financial freedom and social supports can expect to raise the child and not worry about her financial well-being for what may have been an unplanned pregnancy. In addition, Mannie Fresh wants us to know that he is not forcing himself sexually on these women—often it’s assumed that if women are in a coerced sexual relationship they would voice their concerns, but this has been shown in multiple analyses to be a flawed interpretation. Mannie Fresh does not consider the relationship any further and is satisfied with his conclusion that if the women did not want to have sex with him, and in some cases, bare his children then they would not do so.

Analysis of sexuality in late twentieth century New Orleans in this song mirrors nineteenth-century French authors like Balzac, Stendhal, and Flaubert who extensively explored the intersections of sexuality and the French bourgeoisie in their novels. The authors of these novels have been criticized for minimizing the agency and consideration of structures of power that make it hard for women to truly choose. Mannie Fresh makes a similar half-considered conclusion that ladies are “without no drama.”
There is a coincidental through-line from Old World France to New World France in New Orleans, Louisiana. The Cash Money Millionaires are a group based out of New Orleans, USA. There has been much analysis of extra-marital sex in French culture particularly when the initial release of Madame Bovary by Gustave Flaubert was blocked by censors and the controversy propelled sales of the book; likewise, 1990s rap in USA resulted in legal and moral concerns that it would corrupt listeners and bring the downfall of traditional family structure. Broader still, in male-dominated societies, and particularly those that value “rugged individualism” it is a nearly universal condition that men have more money and power, while women, when described by men, are subservient and their needs and wants are minimized. History repeats itself.
While the French authors concluded that open sexuality may cause society break down, the Cash Money Millionaires are not concerned that these relationships will cause problems for society. Their tone is positive, playful, and boastful.
Mannie may not share as whole-heartedly with the others in his celebration of a male fantasy that objectifies women. In many cases, a double negative is used to suggest that there is something other than the quality that is being described—Mannie Fresh states “without no drama.” A lack of “drama” does not mean there are no misgivings or concerns about the nature of these sexual and romantic relationships. In the next line, Mannie Fresh may actually be requesting that “niggas with figgas” to say “I love my baby mama.” Perhaps Mannie Fresh is asking others to regard women more fully than the consideration that they are typically afforded. Other analysts of Mannie Fresh note that he tends to focus on positive relationships, so it’s possible that Mannie Fresh is conceding that while the rest of the song will describe sexual acts women provide to the men that the focus should be on love and lasting connection, rather than lust or power.

It’s worth considering that the entire song is likely self-aware that they are of low socioeconomic status, but similar relationships exist in high socioeconomic status relationships. The rappers describe their relationship with women with enthusiasm and playful regard. Powerful and rich men, some of the wealthiest in the world, also describe their relationship with women in matter-of-fact ways that when regarding the women demonstrates their second-class status. It’s hard not to consider a harem of women serving a plutocrat, or sheik in the same way that the Cash Money Millionaires describe what sounds like a constant flow of mostly unnamed women.
Is the relationship between the Cash Money Millionaires really that different or more objectifying than men from more “respectable society,” or those that live in France or Saudi Arabia, for example, or who lived 150 to 200 years ago?

line: She hate that we can get loose But I can never hang tight
vault_lines: She hate that we can get loose
meaning:
Wayne’s girlfriend (“she”) is upset that Wayne seems always willing to “get loose,” but not to “hang tight.” This is susceptible to at least two meanings (depending on which phrase we interpret first).

Meaning 1: To “get loose” means to relax and take things easy. In this context, “hanging tight” is the negative form of “get loose,” and it means doing all of the serious, necessary things to make a relationship work and be healthy.

Meaning 2: To “hang tight” means to wait patiently. In this context, to “get loose” is the negative form of “hang tight,” and it might mean several things, such as igniting arguments, engaging in intercourse, or consuming drugs/alcohol—all of which Wayne struggles to resist in the face of strong temptations.

line: So retreat, or suffer defeat
vault_lines: So retreat, or suffer defeat
meaning:
In the line “I’m me, times three”, Lil Wayne makes a recursive reference to himself being three times himself.  Of course, if we resolve that reference, we again must multiple Lil Wayne * 3 ad infinitum.  In computer science, the integer then overflows, writing to unexpected areas of memory, causing undefined behavior.  This is obviously dangerous, thus Lil Wayne here is making a clever nod to himself being dangerous.  This is confirmed in the next line: “So retreat, or suffer defeat.”

Lil Wayne is essentially threatening to defeat his foe by causing a buffer overflow; dangerous indeed!

Reader Question: Why is a goon nothing compared to a goblin? And are the Raiders the Goons of the NFL and the Titans the Goblins?

Hip-hop reflectionist and sociologist Michael Eric Dyson recited these two lines during a panel at Brown University, explaining why they’re important in hip-hop:

[It] is an interesting couplet because it gives rise to the post-industrial incarceration of African-American and Latino men disproportionately […] That incarceration cannot, in any stretch of the imagination, be ascribed to the preoccupation within rap lyrics and the glorification of prison as the locus classicus for the primary spot, for the development of Black identity, as the ideal spot with which Blackness can be located. meaning:
Drake is known for his admiration for the city of Houston, Texas. Ever since his career began, the Toronto native has paid homage to Houston in his music; his 2009 track “November 18th” is influenced by the music of legendary Houston producer DJ Screw. His song “Houstonlantavegas” is also a tribute, in part, to the city.

Drake makes wordplay out of “Houston” and references Whitney Houston, the iconic pop/R&B singer who became famous for hits such as “I Will Always Love You” and “I Wanna Dance With Somebody” before her untimely drug-related death on February 11, 2012.

Additionally, “Whitney” is a slang term for cocaine. Whitney Houston was known for her drug use, and it is believed that cocaine played a role in her death. Drake also name-checks pop singer Britney Spears and actress Lindsay Lohan, both of whom have been known in the past for their drug abuse, with both of their names serving as slang terms to cocaine.



Although Drake has admitted to drug usage in the past, the rapper has primarily stayed away from drugs. In a 2019 Rap Radar interview, Drake claimed to not be doing any drugs.

line: They say I’m trippin’, I guess they wishin’ I finally fall
vault_lines: They say I'm trippin', I guess they wishin' I finally fall
meaning:
The colloquial term “trippin'” is a multifaceted choice of words. Commonly used in informal speech, “trippin'” often refers to someone acting in an irrational, unreasonable, or unusual manner. It’s a phrase that encapsulates a deviation from the norm, suggesting a loss of the usual composure or rationality.

However, in the clever hands of Lil Wayne, “trippin'” does more than describe erratic behavior. It becomes a bridge to the imagery of physically stumbling or falling. This use of “trippin'” carries an implicit anticipation of a mistake or failure, aligning with the literal notion of a fall. The term thus serves a dual purpose: it reflects the accusations of his critics while also setting the stage for the metaphorical fall they anticipate.

line: All I gotta be is all that I can possibly
vault_lines: All I gotta be is all that I can possibly
meaning: Lil Wayne employs a nuanced and inventive rhyming technique that showcases his unique lyrical prowess. Rather than opting for a more conventional phrase like “all I gotta be is all that I can possibly be” or “all I gotta be is all that I can be,” Wayne cleverly merges these ideas into a singular, impactful expression. He does this by placing a distinctive emphasis on the syllable “bly” in “possibly,” creating an auditory illusion where “possibly” simultaneously evokes the sound of “possibly be.” This intricate play on words and sounds demonstrates Wayne’s skill in manipulating language and rhythm, creating a layered and sophisticated rhyme that may not be immediately apparent in text but becomes strikingly evident when heard.

line: Choppin’ up a lil’ cash cow, that’s steak I’m eatin’
vault_lines: Choppin' up a lil' cash cow, that's steak I'm eatin'
meaning: The phrase “cash cow,” a common metaphor for a consistent source of profit, is ingeniously juxtaposed with the literal concept of “steak,” a product derived from a cow. This juxtaposition is not merely a play on words but a layered representation of success and wealth. By “chopping up” the metaphorical cash cow, the artist symbolically enjoys the fruits of his labor, represented by the “steak.” The pun relies on the word “steak” serving as both a literal reference to a cut of beef and a homophone for “stake,” meaning a share or investment in a venture. By using “steak,” Wayne cleverly alludes to both the tangible rewards of his success (eating a literal steak) and the financial gains from his investments (having a stake in a “cash cow” business).

Throughout the years, elements of bounce music have been incorporated in the works of many different artists, including Wayne and Drake themselves; the former’s contributions have helped turn several bounce-inspired songs (such as “A Milli” and Juvenile’s “Back That A** Up”) into nationwide hits, while the latter paid tribute to the genre on his 2019 song “Nice For What,” which even features a short introduction by Big Freedia herself.

“Fee-fi-fo-fum” is the first line of a historical quatrain (or sometimes couplet) famous for its use in the classic English fairy tale “Jack and the Beanstalk”. The poem, as given in Joseph Jacobs' 1890 rendition, is as follows:

Fee-fi-fo-fum,
I smell the bones of an Englishman,
Be he alive, or be he dead
I’ll grind his bones
And get his dough.

Though the rhyme is tetrametric, it follows no consistent metrical foot; however, the lines correspond roughly to a monosyllabic tetrameter, a dactylic tetrameter, a trochaic tetrameter, and an iambic tetrameter respectively. The poem has historically made use of assonant half rhyme.

line: And if the shoe fits, wear it, I can’t if these not new
vault_lines: And if the shoe fits, wear it, I can't if these not new
meaning:
Lil Wayne rhetorically and metaphorically challenges other rappers to try on his “shoes” to see if they fit.

And if the shoe fits, wear it; I can’t if these not new

He is telling them that if they think they’re truly capable of being like him (“if the shoe fits”), they should do it (“wear it”). He presents this as a win-win test of his own greatness:
(1) the widespread inability of others to imitate him serves as proof of his uniqueness and superiority [the rhetorical challenge];
(2) the rare few who can successfully follow his blueprint will elevate themselves in the rap game [the metaphorical challenge], thus making them Wayne’s “mini-mes."

At the same time, Wayne makes clear that—literally and metaphorically—he will not wear “shoes” unless they are brand new (“… wear it; I can’t if these not new”):
Literal meaning: He will never put on previously-worn footwear because of his wealth and high standards.
Metaphorical meaning: He refuses to copy another person’s fashion/rapping style/etc. because he is always original.

Critically, Wayne revives this  “shoe” metaphor later in the song by explaining the types of “shoes” he wears and the “steps” he takes, representing important aspects of his life that have contributed to his superstar image/persona. Through this explanation, Wayne offers genuine “instructions” on how to be like him (and achieve success) while knowing his instructions are nearly impossible to replicate fully:

Young nigga from the hood with a plan
One foot in the street, one foot in the sand
One foot in the cleats, one foot in the Vans
One foot in your ass, one fourth of a Xan
Follow my footsteps—I’ll give you instructions

Note: View the annotation under the later lyric “I give you instructions” for an explanation of the three instructions Wayne provides to other rappers.

line: I give you instructions
vault_lines: I give you instructions
meaning:
Follow my footsteps—I’ll give you instructions

Wayne is literally giving “instructions” to other rappers on how to “be like [him]"—that is, to be successful in the rap industry. This mirrors his portrayal of a doctor on the 2008 track Dr. Carter, where he saves the life of a dying hip-hop genre by diagnosing the flaws in other rappers and delivering the cures through his verses.

In the previous three lines, Wayne uses literal footsteps in specific places to illustrate the metaphorical “steps” he took to achieve success. These three metaphorical “steps” form the basis for three “instructions” that, if followed by other rappers, will help them to achieve commercial and financial success:

One foot in the streets, one foot in the sand

Instruction #1: Understand how to connect with the streets and the suburbs (the “sand” invokes images of beaches and luxury) to maximize the size of your audience.

One foot in the cleats, one foot in the Vans

Instruction #2: Some athletes (specifically, football and soccer players) must wear cleats in their respective sports. Here, the “game” that Wayne participates in is the rap game, so having “one foot in the cleats" means one should always be connected to, and continue for as long as one can, their rapping. In contrast, putting “one foot in the Vans” means one should have personal interests and business ventures outside of rapping. For Wayne, these include sports and skating, explaining his references to “cleats” and “Vans,” specifically (Wayne owns a sports agency and, around a week after Be Like Me was released, he collaborated with Vans on a marketing campaign).

One foot in your ass, one-fourth of a Xan

Instruction #3: Be a “foot in the ass” of other rappers and take drugs for inspiration and vulnerability (but not too many drugs).

line: The motherfuckin’ best yet, sorry for cussin’ (Who?)
vault_lines: The motherfuckin' best yet, sorry for cussin' (Who?)
meaning:
Back when Lil Wayne had started rapping for Cash Money his parent approved of his passion for being a rapper and let him rap alongside them, being that he was around the age of thirteen when this started, they asked one condition of him, and that was that he was not allowed to use any cuss words in his songs.

It wasn’t until his song Fuck The World when he decided it was time to make an exception to the rule. The only reason he used the word was to emphasize his emotional power in the song.

Producer Mannie Fresh had this to say on the subject:

“I don’t even know if he remembers this but, we had a conversation and Wayne was just like, ‘I feel like I’m old enough now. I wanna curse. I’d rather not be a hypocrite and be cursing by myself.’ I’m asked him, ‘What’s the idea?’ He says ‘Well, I got this song that I wanna do and it’s kind of heartfelt so it’s gotta be like that.’ That’s when he did ‘Fuck the World.’”

In the chorus of the song he even states that he doesnt use foul language

I don’t curse, but in this verse, man, fuck the world"

Futhermore Lil Wayne mentioned he would NEVER use foal language in his raps back then in an interview with Kronick Magazine:

[Y]ou don’t cuss on the records. What’s up with that? Is it still like that?
It’ll always be like that. [… My mom] don’t play that. That’s why I don’t curse. […] Man, I could turn 35. It ain’t gon' happen."

We now know that didn’t quite happen, and six years later by the time Tha Carter 2 was released he had been using profanity in large. This line is a shout-out, and apology, to his parents, since who else would he be apologizing to for using the ‘F’ word seven times in a row at the start of this very verse, the same cuss word he used in his raps for the first time back then.

meaning:
Wayne tightly layers a set of cultural and historical references. The phrase “Jackie red” likely nods to Jacqueline Kennedy, whose iconic red outfits were highlighted in the 2016 film Jackie (2016 film). Meanwhile, “Julie blonde” evokes Julie Andrews, whose bright blonde look in The Sound of Music (film) remains part of its legendary imagery. Both figures epitomize facets of the 1960s cultural landscape.

By describing them as “Cuban fine,” Wayne invokes the high-end aura of Cuban cigars, long associated with luxury, exclusivity, and restricted access. Yet the phrase subtly alludes to the Cuban Missile Crisis—a defining geopolitical event of the Kennedy era. Before imposing the U.S. trade embargo against Cuba, John F. Kennedy secretly secured 1,200 Cuban cigars for himself, highlighting the intersection of indulgence and prohibition.

Wayne’s next line, “I bruise they spine,” initially reads as a straightforward sexual boast. However, within the Cold War subtext, it also parallels the bruising of American pride during the Cuban Missile Crisis. Just as Wayne’s presence leaves a lasting, almost visceral impact on his partners, the U.S. suffered a psychological and strategic “bruising” upon discovering that Soviet nuclear warheads had been deployed just 90 miles off its shores—a direct penetration of its sphere of influence.

The following phrase, “I leave and they snooze ‘til nine,” deepens the historical connection. While the lyric suggests Wayne departing before his partners awaken, it also mirrors the U.S.’s delayed awareness of the missile threat. On October 16, 1962, at approximately 9 AM, Kennedy was briefed on Soviet missile sites in Cuba—marking the moment the U.S. “woke up” to the reality of its precarious situation. Just as Wayne’s partners remain unaware of his absence until later, the U.S. was effectively “asleep” to the nuclear threat until the moment of discovery.

This interplay between pleasure and peril, secrecy and revelation, indulgence and restriction reflects a broader theme in Wayne’s lyricism—the duality of wealth and limitation. Much like Kennedy securing cigars before restricting them for others, Wayne embodies the paradox of having access to luxury yet remaining aware of forces that limit true autonomy—whether in relationships, industry, or power dynamics.

Ultimately, these lines exemplify Wayne’s signature allusiveness, seamlessly blending historical depth with braggadocio, turning a moment of sexual dominance into a reflection on Cold War tensions and the fragility of power.

line: Now, who am I? I’m who and why I’m rude and kind, my cars are computerized
vault_lines: Now, who am I? I'm who and why
I'm rude and kind, my cars are computerized
meaning: Wayne uses a rhetorical inversion reminiscent of Shakespeare’s “Fair is foul, and foul is fair.” from Macbeth. He collapses identity (“Who am I?”) and purpose (“Why am I?”) into one self-defining statement, “I’m who and why”, presenting himself as both question and answer. Wayne then moves from the broad, almost nebulous question of identity and purpose (blending “who” and “why”) to the intermediate claim, “I’m rude and kind,”—less abstract, yet still open to interpretation as both gangster swagger (“rude boy”) and personal contradiction. Finally, he narrows to a highly specific flex with, “My cars are computerized.” This progression—philosophical, behavioral, then material—forms a spectrum of braggadocio, illustrating how Wayne seamlessly condenses cosmic self-definition into concrete, tech-forward boasting in the span of a few quick bars.

meaning:
Here, Wayne presents the issue (“the puzzle”) of the government trying to prevent him and his people from speaking or acting (putting them “in a muzzle,” like  an unruly dog). As a metaphor, Wayne likens this issue to an incomplete puzzle.

“But your two fingers ain’t the pieces to the puzzle,” is a double entendre that serves to dispel two potential solutions to this issue (in keeping with the metaphor, Wayne explains that these two “puzzle pieces” cannot solve the incomplete puzzle):

(1) By holding up two fingers—in particular, the index and middle fingers—a person makes the “peace” sign. [Wayne subtly reveals the meaning of “two fingers” by using “piece” as a homophone for “peace.”]. Wayne does not believe that a peaceful response will solve the issue of governmental oppression.

(2) Moreover, this bar suggests that solving the issue might require a collective, rather than individual, response. Wayne explains that effort is futile when the only actors attempting to make a difference are “[you and] your two fingers.”

In 2007, police discovered a .40-caliber handgun (registered to Wayne’s manager) in Wayne’s tour bus during a search prompted by the smell of marijuana. Wayne was eventually sentenced to one year in federal prison after pleading guilty to attempted criminal possession of a weapon—this made him a felon who can no longer legally possess a firearm.

In 2008, while Wayne’s tour bus was stopped at a U.S. Border Patrol checkpoint in Arizona, officers discovered drugs, cash, and a .40-caliber handgun (registered to Wayne). Wayne eventually pleaded guilty to one count of drug possession, while the weapons charge was dismissed (due to a potentially illegal search of the tour bus).

In 2019, federal agents searched Wayne’s private jet after receiving a tip, finding drugs and a gold-plated .45-caliber handgun (which was unregistered). Wayne pleaded guilty to possession of a firearm and ammunition by a convicted felon but, on January 19, 2021, was issued a total and complete pardon for these crimes by President Donald Trump, avoiding punishment.

Practice the code of silence, omérta

meaning:
Omérta, roughly translating to “humility” in Italian, is the code and oath of silence about criminal activity and a refusal to give evidence to authorities practiced by the Sicilian Mafia among other Italian groups. A break in the code is punishable by death, and in some cases the death of the perpetrator’s family. Omérta can be summarized as such:

Cu è surdu, orbu e taci, campa cent'anni ‘mpaci

Or in English:

He who is deaf, blind, and silent will live a hundred years in peace

Gudda compares the Italian oath to that of the “street code,” where snitching is punishable by death in the same manner. Drake likened himself with the code of Omérta in a similar way with his 2019 track, “Omertà”:

Ethics and values, mob traditions, old fashioned
…

Racketeering, the syndicate got they hand in plenty things
The things that we’ve done to protect the name are unsettling

meaning:
The chorus starts off with a reference to two Kid Cudi songs from his debut album Man on the Moon: The End of Day: “Enter Galactic (Love Connection Part I)” and “Sky Might Fall.” Coincidentally, Cudi also mentioned “the dark side of the moon” on his song “Soundtrack 2 My Life,” which is also from the same album:

I live in a cocoon opposite of Cancun
Where it is never sunny, the dark side of the moon

The Dark Side of the Moon is the 1973 classic album by Pink Floyd and is one of their most popular albums—selling over 75 million copies, making it one of the best selling albums of all time. In their context, Nicki and Wayne use “the dark side of the moon” as a metaphor for one’s low point in life. No matter how hard life is, they will be there for their significant other.

In reality, there’s no such thing as the “dark side of the moon”—the correct term is “far side of the moon,”  as both sides of the moon get the same amount of sunlight.

Wayne has a long history of referring to himself in extraterrestrial terms, with the Martian usually being his alien race of choice.

It’s one of the most commonly recurring lyrical motifs of his career and culminated in him naming an entire album, I Am Not a Human Being, based on the concept in 2010, which he then followed up with a sequel three years later.

The implication of his ongoing assertion that he is not from this planet is, presumably, that he believes his own talent to be quite simply out of this world, a point which he underlines by describing his competition in religious terms as sacrificial lambs to the slaughter, being offered up as testament to his God-like lyrical ability.



Wayne himself, given his status as one of the most important emcees of modern times, is more than likely a hugely influential figure to many of the newer crop of artists whom he appears to be a taking down a notch here, a fact that he is apparently all too aware of, but which doesn’t appear to diminish his disappointment in them.

He likens his indirect tutelage of the younger generation to them receiving an Ivy League education from Harvard University, widely considered one of the worlds most prestigious seats of learning, an education which he, evidently, feels they have wasted.

Whilst its unclear whether he has anybody in particular in mind, Wayne appears to be taking aim at the newer crop of emcees here, who he evidently feels are lacking in comparison to him.

He states that his own musical output is “retarded”, a multi-faceted word with a plethora of meanings, which in this context is being used to denote something which is impressive, specifically in an outlandish or overt manner, which would certainly correlate with the praise heaped on Weezy’s lyrical ability over the years.

In comparison he describes his competitors as sweet, which in this context would be synonymous with something soft and not to be taken seriously, and continues the sweetness metaphor by cleverly conjuring the image of a tart, a sugary, tangy type of desert.

He then immediately follows up by stating that he himself goes tart, invoking a lesser known meaning of the same word which roughly means to speak in a quick, sharp and often nasty manner.

He doubles up on the potentially unpleasant nature of what’s taking place here by comparing this particular lyrical onslaught the physical act of throwing up, which implies not only that he’s letting everything out but that he’s physically disgusted by the state of the rap game as it exists at the moment

vault_lines: 'Cause I'm high like a bitch, yeah I'm high like a bitch

meaning:
Clever play on words with what is called minimal pairs. The consonants p and b are both bilabial sounds, that is, both are produced with the help of both lips, with the only difference that b is a sound consonant (that is, a consonant that makes your vocal chords vibrate when you produce the sound) and p is a mute consonant (the type of consonant that doesn’t make your vocal chords vibrate), try and do it and you’ll see.

So, for being both bilabials, stop consonants and having an important distinctive characteristic (one is sound and the other one is mute), these two consonants are what is called a minimal pair, that is, two consonants that create an important distinction in between the meaning of two words, such as what we have in here, pitch and bitch. This is what creates the amusing effect of this couplet.

Also, there is the double entendre of the word high:


A musical pitch can be high or low. This ties in with being high like Mariah Carey cause shes known for highting some pretty high notes

line: Eyes stay tight like Chinese Connection
vault_lines: Eyes stay tight like Chinese Connection
meaning:
I stay tight like Chinese Connection

This multi-layered bar illustrates Wayne’s fashion sense and swagger. “I stay tight” means that he ensures his clothing and demeanor are always stylish.

On the surface, Wayne employs a kind of rhetorical tautology, likening his “tight[ness]” to a “connection”  because a connection is defined by tight linkage, reinforcing the idea of tightness (i.e., stylishness) through repetition.

Digging deeper, Chinese Connection is an alternate name for the martial arts film titled Fist of Fury, released in 1972. The film takes place in China and, thus, many of the actors are Chinese including the film’s star, Bruce Lee.



Understanding this context reveals a subtle homophone:

Eye stay tight like Chinese Connection.

Wayne is saying that he is as tight (i.e., stylish) as the eyes of the actors in the film Chinese Connection are tight (see the “almond-shaped” eyes that westerners commonly associate with the people of China).

Additionally, Wayne’s heavy drug use, including the “downers” of marijuana and lean that make the user drowsy, is crucial to his rap star image. This bar suggests that his nearly-shut eyes often resemble those of the actors in Chinese Connection, an important element of his signature nonchalant demeanor.

Finally, in law enforcement and street terminology, a “Chinese connection” refers to heroin trafficking networks linked to China-based suppliers. The phrase evokes organized infrastructure, tightly run supply chains, and dependable sourcing. By invoking this imagery, Wayne suggests that he is just as tight (i.e., stylish) as these networks are meticulously organized and operated.

Though the first written form of Peter Piper dates back to 1813 in Peter Piper’s Practical Principles of Plain and Perfect Pronunciation by John Harris, many suspect the rhyme was said earlier than that.

It is believed that “Peter Piper” refers to Pierre Poivre. A French horticulturist, Pierre was responsible for growing many plants from foreign, including spices such as cloves.

The tongue-twister reads as the following:

line: They say numbers don’t lie except one-time
vault_lines: They say numbers don't lie except one-time
meaning:
Wayne is effectively saying: “numbers don’t lie, except when they do.”

It is a common saying that “numbers don’t lie,” meaning that factual data unbiased by human intervention typically represents the truth. However, another common saying that typically follows an absolute claim is: “…, except when [the absolute] doesn’t happen.” This is a comedic, realistic way of viewing the world where nothing is absolute, and any outcome is possible at all times.

Moreover, he cleverly identifies the specific amount of times the numbers will lie: “one time.” However, this itself could be an instance of numbers lying, as numbers could easily lie on more than one occasion. Possibly, Wayne is demonstrating the effect of human intervention on statistics, as the source of the “one time” conclusion is “[t]hey say.”

Finally, when people complain about the “one time” something occurs, that occurrence is typically at a crucial point in time, adding to the stress of the situation (c'est la vie).

Then, in classic Weezy fashion, he flips the tone with “Anybody seen the roof to the top of my car?” a flex hidden in a question. He’s saying his car is a convertible, there’s literally no roof. It doubles as a metaphor: there’s no ceiling on what he can achieve, and also no protection from the elements (i.e., fame, scrutiny, mental strain). The line plays on the duality of wealth and vulnerability, one second he’s on top, the next he’s exposed.

It’s a brilliant juxtaposition: vulnerability meets braggadocio, pain meets punchline.

vault_lines: We greedy fuckers, eat your supper, pick our teeth, and mug you
The pockets bustin' out the muscle, bitch, I'm bleedin' blubber
meaning:
Wayne artfully employs gastronomic metaphor and sardonic wit to articulate a narrative of rapacious dominance, infusing it with a macabre whimsy that renders the imagery both grotesque and darkly playful. The phrase “We greedy fuckers, eat your supper, pick our teeth, and mug you” transcends mere verbal imagery; it becomes an allegory for the insatiable acquisition of power and resources. The act of consuming ‘your supper’ is not just literal ingestion but a metaphorical usurpation of what belongs to another. This is followed by a casual, almost disdainful gesture of picking one’s teeth—an action that denotes both satisfaction and a dismissive disregard for the consumed. The subsequent progression to ‘mugging’ encapsulates a transition from metaphorical consumption to direct aggression, portraying a predatory nature that is both unflinching and remorseless, yet tinged with a sinister playfulness.

Continuing this vivid portrayal, the line “The pockets bustin' out the muscle, bitch, I’m bleedin' blubber” further embellishes the theme of corporeal excess and opulence with an element of whimsical grotesquerie. Here, the imagery shifts from the act of consuming to the physical embodiment of its consequences. The pockets, straining against muscular confines, serve as a potent metaphor for wealth that is not just ample but excessively burdensome. The phrase “bleedin' blubber,” with its visceral connotations, evokes an image of overflowing, almost pathological affluence. The use of ‘blubber'—a term often associated with the excess body fat of marine mammals—introduces an eerie, carnival-esque exaggeration, amplifying the sense of overindulgence and prodigality with a darkly humorous flourish.

Wayne’s multifaceted wordplay serves two primary functions:

Literal Implications of “Repercussion”: Wayne warns of the direct consequences of negative actions or behaviors—talking disrespectfully can lead to physical retaliation or robbery, and excessive selfishness might lead to one’s downfall.

Musical Reference to “Percussion”: On another level, Wayne integrates the concept of “percussion” into his lyrics and delivery. He repeatedly uses the term “beat” not just in its literal sense of physically beating but also to refer to musical rhythm. line: These ain’t songs, these is hymns ’cause I’m him It’s the Psalm 151, this New Testament The book of Hov (The book of Hov) Jesus turned water to wine, for Hov, it just took a stove

Jesus turned water to wine, for Hov, it just took a stove
meaning:
Psalms is a book containing lyrics to ancient Hebrew religious hymns included as part of the Christian Old Testament as well as the Jewish Tanakh. In Christian and Jewish tradition, there are only 150 Psalms – hence Hov (also a religious reference – Jay-hova / “Jehovah”, a name for the Abrahamic God) is writing the 151st, his own hymn to his miraculous success. He then escalates this to a new New Testament and picks out a title for the new Bible book about him.

The New Testament of the Christian Bible is concerned with the teachings of Jesus Christ, who, as the second person in the Trinity, is God – God can be referred to as “Him” or “He”, which is the sense in which Jay uses it in “hymns ‘cause I’m Him”. Hov’s comparing himself to Jesus, who turned water to wine at a party in the way Hov miraculously turned cooking crack on the stove into a business empire.

A real “Psalm 151” does exist in the Septuagint, an early Greek translation of the Old Testament that includes parts later excised. The Psalm is written from the point of view of David, celebrating his victory over Goliath, and praising God for choosing him to become a great leader over his tall, better-looking brothers – thematically similar to the story Jay is recounting in “GOD DID”.

God anointed me with holy oil;
God made me leader for his people,
ruler over the children
of his covenant.

line: Some new niggas out of pocket, talkin’ exotic You barely been to the Baham— (Haha) that’s another topic

You barely been to the Baham— (Haha) that's another topic
meaning:
The line starts out with some wordplay – out of pocket is a phase that means either losing money in a transaction, or behaving inappropriately. Hov suggests his poor enemies/obnoxious haters are so far out of the pocket that they’re exotic, then plays that association into the exotic holiday destination of the Bahamas – while most people would be happy to spend a week in a hotel there, the Carters have their own island. Exotic is also slang for marijuana, transitioning from the weed theme of the previous bars.

Hov then playfully cuts off his association because he remembers the Bahamas are a tax haven. Citizens of the Bahamas do not pay tax on income or capital gains and foreign businesses can be incorporated there. This has made the Bahamas the third richest country in the Americas, after the USA and Canada.

While tax avoidance is legal, it’s an exploitation of loopholes that goes against what taxation is supposed to achieve – to keep money in the local economy and pay for infrastructure that businesses use to achieve their fortunes in the first place. Hov’s change of topic is a joking attempt to correct bringing up a dirty secret. Topic may be a pun on tropics.

The Bahamas were also a popular place for sourcing illicit drugs, though Jay-Z’s own connect was in St. Thomas.

Monogram is the name of Jay-Z’s luxury medicinal marijuana brand. On the red carpet, stars usually dress up in suits and tuxedos. It’s not uncommon for a gentleman to have a pocket square with his initials monogrammed on them.

Record is a double entendre for recorded music, sometimes pressed onto vinyl records. Lil Wayne once claimed that he invented the (now famous) term, “bling-bling”.



However, the ideophone of light hitting jewelry came to usage before Wayne was even born!

During the mid- to late 1960s, toothpaste maker Ultra Brite ran a series of commercials stating, “Ultrabrite gives your mouth… [PING]… sex appeal!”; the “ping” represented a bell-like sound when the young man/woman smiled in the commercial.

Jesse West (aka 3rd Eye) is cited as perhaps the first rapper to use the complete term “bling bling”, in Supercat’s 1993 hit, “Dolly My Baby (Remix)”.

On another note, older comedians (i.e. Martin Lawrence) eventually parodied the “Ultrabrite smile” by vocalizing the sound effect as both “bling-bling,” and “bling-blauw.” Ever watch Martin)? One of his several alter-egos was a man named Jerome who had a rotten gold-toothed smile and stereotypical pimp jewelry.

meaning:
This is a brilliant metaphor that combines two folk sayings (or axioms of life) into a single, coherent narrative:
1. If you ignore your problems without addressing them, those problems will only become larger, and things will eventually reach a tipping point where the now-massive problems can no longer be ignored.
2. If you try to hide facts about yourself (especially unfavorable facts), you are creating “skeletons in your closet.” Learning about these “skeletons” will shock someone who knows you.

Wayne is saying that if he puts his trouble in his pockets (refuses to acknowledge/address his problems), then hangs up his pants (sets the problems aside completely, or tries to forget about his problems), then he will have created monsters in his closet (hidden facts about Wayne that, if known by his peers, would shock them).

Wayne likely refers to “monsters,” instead of skeletons, to emphasize the gravity and danger of the issues he creates by failing to address his problems. Moreover, while a skeleton is a lifeless arrangement of bones, a monster is a live creature that can harm bystanders. Wayne is saying that someone who “opens his closet” will not merely be shocked at the sight of a “skeleton,” but might actually be harmed by the “monster” Wayne has created.

It is commonly used for the treatment of anxiety disorders, especially of panic disorder, but also in the treatment of generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) or social anxiety disorder. meaning:
Wayne has a deep and extensive history with his old label Cash Money and their owner Birdman. Known as one of the original founders of the group, Weezy joined them at 13.



Wayne and Birdman had a very close relationship since he was signed, and it was very visible with tapes such as, Like Father Like Son. The label was widely successful throughout the 2000s, and when Wayne founded Young Money, their ‘child’ label, business became even more fruitful.

All seemed well before 2014, when Wayne called out Birdman and YMCB for the delayed release of his anticipated Carter V. After tweeting out his frustration, he later stated:

I want off this label and nothing to do with these people but unfortunately it ain’t that easy. I am a prisoner and so is my creativity.
https://twitter.com/LilTunechi/status/540569858287493120?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw&ref_url=http%3A%2F%2Fwww.complex.com%2Fmusic%2Flil-wayne-cash-money-beef-timeline%2F

In 2015, after heavy support from Cortez Bryant, Wayne filed a $51 million lawsuit against the label. He spoke on it during an interview, saying:

It’s super-done. Cake baked, icing on top, name on top, candles lit. I would have released it yesterday if I could. But it’s a dead subject right now. It’s a jewel in the safe. It’s that stash-house money.

He even went as so far as to start a “Fuck Cash Money” chant at one of his shows. Wayne’s Tidal-released Free Weezy Album seemed to confirm his official exit from the label.

Although there was a brief onstage reconciliation, where Birman shouted to his fans:

This my motherfucking son, and I'ma die for him, I'ma live for him, and I’ll motherfucking kill for him. That ain’t never changed. YMCMB for life.

“I’m high as Felicia, baby” may be referring to the popular meme/catchphrase “Bye, Felica.” When someone says “Bye, Felicia” they want to leave a certain situation or leave someone’s presence. meaning:
Mannie’s on the beat and bringing back the classic New Orleans bounce sound—the energetic and 808-heavy beats that Cash Money popularized in the ‘90s. Bounce grew out of the confluence of Miami Bass in the '80s (also a very 808-heavy genre) and the growing  hip-hop influence from New York around the same time. New Orleans had its own hip-hop scene, and Mannie was on the forefront of that movement as an MC and a DJ. He still prefers vintage equipment to the programs that producers use to make beats today.

There’s no way you can think now, there’s no creativity in instruments. Some of the earlier Cash Money songs, we didn’t programme those songs, we played them. If you had to hear it on tape, you’d hear somebody going: “One, two, ready, go!” We played those songs all the way down, that’s what made them good songs. Now you can sequence something and walk away from it. And I think the way, the format of music, is cheap to a certain degree. You’ve got a lot of equipment that’ll do it for you.

Wayne gets cheese (slang for money) like Mickey Mouse.



Wayne continues this line by saying he gets a lot of bucks (also slang for money); however bucks also refers to a shotgun shell.

meaning:
In American football, a touchdown occurs when a team scores behind the other team’s goal line while a field goal occurs when a team kicks the ball over the other team’s uprights during a regular offensive play.

What Wayne’s talking about, however, is conversion, which occurs when the team who scored a touchdown is allowed to try for an extra point by kicking the ball through the other team’s uprights—similarily to a field goal.

The difference between a conversion and a field goal is that a conversion only offers one extra point, in addition to the six points earned from a touchdown while a field goal is three points.

line: Woke up at six (Six), pray to a .9 (.9) Twelve (Twelve), was already runnin’ from twelve, a nigga was flyin’
vault_lines: Woke up at six (Six), pray to a .9 (.9)
Twelve (Twelve), was already runnin' from twelve, a nigga was flyin'
meaning:
Kenny Mason makes a clever use of numbers and their slang meanings for the chorus.

“Six,” while referring to the time of day, could potentially refer to Atlanta Police Department Zone 6 which sits on the east side of Atlanta which notoriously has heavy and abusive police presence.

“.9” refers to a .9mm handgun in which Kenny looks to to keep himself safe.

“Twelve,” in this instance, refers to both an age and “12,” a common slang term for police. The line is insistent that since the age of 12, Kenny found fleeing from police to be a necessity.

Hidden between the lines lies an angel number. Angel numbers are numbers with series of repeating digits (111, 222, 333, etc.) that some believe when seen in various places, it is a divine message from a higher power one believes in. Kenny counts in multiples of 3 in the chorus: 6, 9, and 12. The angel number, 333, is often told to be a sign telling that a guardian angel is besides you. In this instance, the guardian angel would refer to the .9mm handgun Kenny keeps besides him and looks to for protection. Kenny’s belief of numerology would be further displayed upon the release of his mixtape, RUFFS, later in the year which held the track “333 / ATOM.”

The introductory line is also potentially an interpolation of JID’s song, Big Black Truck

Up in the morning at 6:45
When I be up, I be talking to God

Fuck with me with this rap shit, yo (What, what?)
meaning:
The pure enjoyment of knowing that we’re the best shows that nobody can fuck with us. The philosopher Immanuel Kant made the same point:

“For just as we found our own limitation in the immeasurability of nature and the insufficiency of our capacity to adopt a standard proportionate to the aesthetic estimation of the magnitude of its domain, but nevertheless at the same time found in our own faculty of reason another, nonsensible standard, which has that very infinity under itself as a unit against which everything in nature is small, and thus found in our own mind a superiority over nature itself even in its immeasurability [that is, you’re the best at what you do]: likewise the irresistibility of its power certainly makes us, considered as natural beings, recognize our physical powerlessness, but at the same time it reveals a capacity for judging ourselves as independent of it and a superiority over nature on which is grounded a self-preservation of quite another kind than that which can be threatened and endangered by nature outside us, whereby the humanity in our person remains undemeaned even though the human being must submit to that dominion [that is, we can be knocked about by the world, but our humanity – our ability to do the right thing for the right reason – is not subject to the laws of physics, and therefore cannot be endangered, which is to say, nobody can fuck with me]. In this way, in our aesthetic judgment nature is judged as sublime not insofar as it arouses fear, but rather because it calls forth our power (which is not part of nature) to regard those things about which we are concerned (goods, health and life) as trivial, and hence to regard its power (to which we are, to be sure, subjected in regard to these things) as not the sort of dominion over ourselves and our authority to which we would have to bow if it came down to our highest principles and their affirmation or abandonment. Thus nature is here called sublime merely because it raises the imagination to the point of presenting those cases in which the mind can make palpable to itself the sublimity of its own vocation even over nature” (Critique of the Power of Judgment, Ak. 5:261-62) – that is, we experience the a priori enjoyment of knowing – that is, the pure enjoyment of knowing – our own superiority. Kant encourages us to identify with that in us that is supersensible, which is to say, nonphysical: in other words, despite appearances, we in fact have no fuckin' body. Other themes from the same book by Kant emerge below, such as artistic genius (“I’ve been spitting for twenty years”) and its relation to imitation (“All I need is a beat with a DMX sample”).

line: Im fresher than a mufucka Cleaner than a sham And a bitch couldn’t pass me If she crammed
vault_lines: Im fresher than a mufucka
Cleaner than a sham
And a bitch couldn't pass me
meaning:
Lil Wayne deftly employs a pun on the word “pass,” weaving together themes of personal allure and academic effort. On one level, “pass” refers to the inability of a woman to overlook his impressive presence, described vividly as being “fresher than a mufucka” and “cleaner than a sham.” This use of “pass” aligns with the common social understanding of someone being too compelling to be ignored, underscoring Wayne’s self-assured portrayal of his charm and style.

The clever twist emerges with the introduction of “crammed,” shifting “pass” into an academic context. In this realm, “passing” a test or exam often involves “cramming,” or intense last-minute studying. By stating that a woman couldn’t pass him even if she “crammed,” Wayne artfully suggests that no amount of effort, akin to preparing for a challenging exam, would enable her to surpass or resist his allure.

R. Kelly is observing a correlation in the natural world: when he is at the club and purchases a single bottle, he usually has a single model to take home. However — as he observes — when he orders more bottles, he is able to obtain more models.

It is a logical fallacy to assume that correlation implies causation. However, in this case, we might assume that R. Kelly has an extensive sample size and is able to control for confounding variables (club quality, bottle quality, model quality, etc.) and therefore implying that the bottles are indeed leading to the models.

meaning:
On October 22, 2009, Lil Wayne pleaded guilty to attempted criminal possession of a weapon, which stems from a 2007 incident when police found .40 caliber pistol in his possession. After two postponements, on March 8, 2010, Wayne was sentenced to one year in prison, which he served at Rikers Island. On November 4, 2010, after serving eight months of his one-year sentence, Wayne was released.

In April 2010, during Lil Wayne’s incarceration, his friends created a website called Weezy Thanx You, which published letters written by Wayne while he was in prison. The first letter was titled “Gone ‘til November,” in which Wayne was said he thought about his children every day, spent his time working out regularly, and read the Bible on a daily basis.

2 Chainz shouts out an extensive (but incomplete) list of Historically Black Colleges & Universities, or HBCUs. These institutions were founded across the United States after slavery’s 1865 abolition and prior to the Civil Rights Act of 1964. HBCUs were created to provide African Americans with higher education during a period in which they were denied entry to white, segregated universities.

Although the Civil Rights Act ended the founding of HBCUs, most of the existing institutions continued to be active. As of this song’s release, there are 107 active HBCUs.

Of the schools that 2 Chainz mentions, he notably highlights his alma mater, Alabama State University. He attended on an athletic scholarship, playing on its basketball team from 1995 to 1997.

Southern University (Baton Rouge, LA)

Florida A&M University (Tallahassee, FL)

Clark Atlanta University (Atlanta, GA)

Alcorn State University (Lorman, MS)

Texas Southern University (Houston, TX)

Tuskegee University (Tuskegee, AL)

Magnum Research Inc. (MRI) designed and developed the Desert Eagle. The design was further refined by (and was also manufactured by) Israel Military Industries (IMI), until 1995, when MRI shifted the manufacturing contract to Saco Defense, in Saco, Maine. The main drums are an overdriven 808, snapping trap snare and rolling hi-hats. A saw-synth plays throughout the track on top of the 808, adding more grittiness to the beat. Electric guitar is introduced during the hook to give it more power.



Da Honorable C.N.O.T.E. talked about the making of this beat in an interview with Complex Magazine. He stated

I went up to New York for some other shit, and I ended up meeting up with Yams and them. And then they played me that joint. It was real rough too. I was like, ‘Yo, [A$AP Rocky] sound crazy on one! I like that shit. This shit is hard.’ We were going back and forth [in the studio], so that ended up being the single. I didn’t know what it was going to be. I didn’t know if they was gonna keep it or not. I was just listening to it that day. It was just ill, and it ended up being the single, which was amazing. Because then I got to work with Mike Dean, so it was me and Mike Dean up there. Mike Dean playing guitar and shit. That’s producing. That’s the shit that I like. You get everybody in the room and let them work. Shit can happen."

He also talked about his creativity for producing in an interview with HipHopdx. Honorable C.N.O.T.E. stated

Every beat I make I try to make it like two years ahead, like where niggas will be in two years from now. If I played it right now they probably wouldn’t get it but two years from now, from the beats leading up to that, they’ll probably get it. As a producer I feel that you should always try to be ahead of the game. That’s how you be an innovator and have people looking up to what you do as a producer."
